title: Hillel's seven rules
hook: Hillel's rules for reading Torah, later expanded to thirteen

segments.voice: Yesterday, gezerah shavah, and your line: same word, same law. A bridge between verses, received from teachers, never made up on a whim. Today, the man who put that bridge on a list. Day one thousand ninety-seven.

The day before Passover falls on Shabbat, and the leaders of the day, the sons of Bathyra, are stuck. They can't remember whether the Passover offering pushes aside the rules of Shabbat. Someone mentions a newcomer up from Babylonia, a student of the great teachers of the age. They send for him. His name is Hillel. He walks in and starts reasoning: a bridge from a shared word, a light-and-heavy argument, one move after another. They aren't moved. Then he says one more sentence, and everything changes. Hold that. Today, the rules he was using.
screen: `PASSOVER MEETS SHABBAT.` → `SEND FOR THE NEWCOMER.` → `HILLEL REASONS. NO ONE MOVES.`

segments.voice: Hillel's seven rules. The Tosefta, an early collection beside the Mishnah, says Hillel expounded seven rules of reading before the sons of Bathyra. Two you already know: light and heavy, and the same word. Others build a general principle from one verse, or from two; read a general statement together with its particulars; compare a case to a similar one elsewhere; and learn a thing from its context. Let's take that last one, because it's easy to feel. The Ten Commandments say, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "Thou shalt not steal." Ordinary theft is forbidden elsewhere in the Torah. So what is this line doing here? Look at its neighbors: murder and adultery, crimes the Torah treats as capital. The Talmud reads it from its context as stealing a person, kidnapping. Same line, read by the company it keeps. Now the rest of the story. In the Jerusalem Talmud's telling, Hillel's arguments don't move the sons of Bathyra. Then he says: this is what I heard from my teachers, Shemaya and Avtalyon. And they accept him, and make him their leader. Yesterday's limit, lived out: the rules matter, and so does the chain of teachers they come down through. Later comes a longer list: a teaching at the start of the Sifra gives Rabbi Ishmael's thirteen rules for reading Torah, with Hillel's tools among them. Some traditional prayer books print that list in the morning service, so the tools of reading sit right beside the prayers. Rules for reading.
screen: `SEVEN RULES BEFORE THE ELDERS.` · `LEARN A THING FROM ITS CONTEXT.` · `WHAT I HEARD FROM MY TEACHERS.` · `LATER, RABBI ISHMAEL'S THIRTEEN.` · then, large: `RULES FOR READING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to learn one rule: learn a thing from its context. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring back one sentence someone said to you recently that stung, or puzzled you. Hold the words alone for a moment. Now widen the frame. What came right before it? What kind of day were they having? What was sitting next to it? Notice whether the sentence changes when it has its neighbors back. You don't have to decide anything. Just read it in its company. The bell holds the time.
Hillel's seven rules. Seven ways of reading Torah that the Tosefta credits to Hillel, from light and heavy to learning from context, later built on by Rabbi Ishmael's thirteen. Today's word.
Your line: rules for reading. Today, before you react to one message or headline, read the line around it first, and see whether its company changes what it says. Day one thousand ninety-seven.

fork.setup: you're Hillel. you've given the sons of Bathyra a shared-word argument and a light-and-heavy argument, and they still won't accept your answer. what do you say?
options: give them a third, cleverer argument.

fork.reveal: in the Jerusalem Talmud's telling, naming his teachers is what moves them, and they make him their leader. the rules and the chain of teachers go together.

original.note: Hebrew: Hillel, the sage the Tosefta credits with seven rules for reading Torah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of tricks for getting the answer you want from a verse.
what it means: seven named ways of reading Torah, later built on by Rabbi Ishmael's thirteen.

what a scholar hears: Tosefta Sanhedrin 7:11's list, the story of the sons of Bathyra in Yerushalmi Pesachim 6:1 (with a parallel in Bavli Pesachim 66a), and the Baraita of Rabbi Ishmael opening the Sifra.

notes: 'Thou shalt not steal' is cited as Exodus 20:13 in JPS 1917 versification (KJV 20:15); please confirm the verse number in JPS 1917.

The seven rules are summarized from Tosefta Sanhedrin 7:11 (kal vachomer, gezerah shavah, binyan av from one verse, binyan av from two verses, kelal u-ferat, ka-yotze bo be-makom acher, davar ha-lamed me-inyano); please confirm the list and plain-English glosses.
The Pesachim 66a story is condensed: the elders (Bnei Betera / 'sons of Bathyra') did not accept Hillel's arguments until he cited Shemaya and Avtalyon, and then appointed him nasi. Please confirm.
'Ordinary theft is forbidden elsewhere in the Torah' refers to Leviticus 19:11; the kidnapping reading is cited to Sanhedrin 86a. Please confirm.

Editor: in Bavli Pesachim 66a the Bnei Betera appoint Hillel nasi right after his arguments; the version where the arguments fail until he cites Shemaya and Avtalyon is the Jerusalem Talmud, Pesachim 6:1. The voice, myth and fork now say 'the Jerusalem Talmud's telling', and that source was added. 'Elders of Bathyra' changed to 'sons of Bathyra' (bnei Betera) throughout; 'in Jerusalem' cut from the hook; Rabbi Ishmael's list no longer said to be 'building on' Hillel's, and the prayer-book claim softened to 'some traditional prayer books'.
